one_liner: Code-generated batched 1D FP32/FP64 GPU FFT kernels with fused ABFT fault tolerance; matches or beats cuFFT, beats VkFFT.
what_it_does: A PPoPP 2025 research prototype: a Python (PyTorch-based) generator reads per-GPU tuning tables (A100 and T4 only) and emits CUDA kernels for batched, out-of-place, forward complex-to-complex FFTs of power-of-two length 2^1 to 2^25 in float2 or double2. Optional variants add thread-level or threadblock-level algorithm-based fault tolerance (checksum detection and online correction) and error injection for testing. There is no library API: the kernels are reached through a function-pointer table (TurboFFT_Kernel_Entry) and the launch geometry, twiddle table and checksum vector are set up by the benchmark driver main.cu, so using it means lifting that driver code.
how_it_is_fast: Each size gets its own generated kernel chain (one launch up to 2^12 or 2^13 depending on the tuning table, two for mid sizes, three for 2^23-2^25): every thread runs an 8-, 16- or 32-point radix-2 sub-FFT in registers with twiddles emitted as compile-time constants, threads exchange data through shared memory, and the large sizes split into multiple kernels with table twiddles between passes. The paper calls the design architecture-aware, padding-free and template-based, with tile sizes and batch-per-block chosen per GPU from a CSV. Fault tolerance is fused into the same kernels: DFT-matrix checksums are reduced with warp shuffles (two-side ABFT with location encoding), so detection and correction add no extra pass over memory.
when_to_use: Batched small 1D power-of-two C2C FFTs (the paper's best case is problems under about 2 MB) on an A100 or T4, where cuFFT kernel choice is weak and launch-bound sizes dominate.

Long-running HPC or ML jobs on GPUs where silent data corruption matters and you want error detection and correction inside the FFT at the 7-15% overhead the paper reports, instead of offline recomputation.
As a starting point for your own fused FFT kernels (the code generator is about 780 lines of Python and the later commits fuse FFT with GEMM for Fourier neural operators).
Reproducing or extending the PPoPP 2025 TurboFFT experiments against cuFFT and VkFFT.
when_not_to_use: You need a drop-in cuFFT replacement: there is no plan/exec API, no inverse or real-to-complex transform, no 2D/3D, no strides, and only power-of-two lengths up to 2^25 ('We currently only support radix-2').
GPUs other than A100 and T4 or architectures other than sm_75/sm_80: CMake rejects any other ARCH_SM value and tuning tables exist only for those two GPUs.
Large transforms where cuFFT is already bandwidth-bound: the claim is 'comparable to or up to 300% faster', with the big gains limited to certain small sizes.
Production use without a maintainer: 9 stars, no releases, no issues filed; the last code commit is from February 2025 (TurboFNO work) and the June 2026 commit only added the Apache-2.0 LICENSE.
Builds without Python: kernels must be generated with Python >= 3.9 and PyTorch before compiling.

integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (cudart; the driver also links cuFFT and cuBLAS), NVIDIA cuda-samples Common helpers via the CUDA_SAMPLES_COMMON environment variable, Python >= 3.9 with PyTorch >= 2.4 and NumPy for code generation; Matplotlib/Seaborn only for plots
integration.min_toolchain: GCC >= 11.2.0, CMake >= 3.24.3 (README; CMakeLists asks for 3.17), CUDA 12.0 for A100 or 11.6 for T4
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs, sm_80 (A100) or sm_75 (T4) only; Linux shell scripts
integration.thread_safety: not documented; kernels are stateless launches on the default stream (no stream parameter in the driver)

gotchas: Benchmark asymmetry: test_turbofft launches the kernel chain once as a warm-up before the timed loop, but test_cufft starts timing on the first cufftExecC2C/Z2Z with no warm-up, and both average over only ntest = 10 runs; any first-call cost lands in cuFFT's number, which matters most for the small sizes where the up-to-300% gains are claimed.

Both timing loops call cudaDeviceSynchronize after every launch inside the event-timed region, and TurboFFT does so after each of its 1-3 kernels, so per-launch host latency is included in all reported times.

At HEAD, run_A100.sh has the codegen, build, 24 benchmark runs, VkFFT build and plotting all commented out (only the newer fft_codegen_stride scripts run); reproducing the paper's A100 figures needs the PPoPP artifact archive (Zenodo record 14220293) or manual uncommenting. run_T4.sh is still complete.
Correctness check in the driver compares against cuFFT with a 1e-4 bound on |diff| / (1 + |ref|), so small-magnitude outputs are effectively checked in absolute rather than relative error.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TurboFFT over VkFFT when you need FP32/FP64 power-of-two batched FFTs on A100/T4 with built-in fault tolerance or the last bit of small-size throughput; pick VkFFT for arbitrary sizes, R2C, inverse, multi-dimensional transforms or non-NVIDIA GPUs, and tcFFT only for FP16 tensor-core work.
verified_claims_summary: The PPoPP 2025 paper (arXiv 2412.05824) reports that TurboFFT without fault tolerance is comparable to, or on certain sizes up to 300% faster than, cuFFT and faster than VkFFT, and that its fault tolerance costs 7-15% even under hundreds of injected errors per minute, for FP32 and FP64 batched 1D C2C FFTs. The artifact README gives the setup: A100-SXM4-40GB with AMD EPYC 7713, GCC 12.3.0, CUDA 12.0; and Tesla T4 with Xeon Silver 4216, GCC 11.2.0, CUDA 11.6; nvcc -O3 -lineinfo with sm_80/sm_75; timings are cudaEvent averages over 10 runs.
status_note: Dormant research artifact (last code commit February 2025, Apache-2.0 LICENSE added June 2026); permissively licensed and copyable, but expect to adapt the generator and driver yourself rather than link a library.
